chunks: As for what Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn Maḥbūb narrated from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from al-Ḥasan ibn Maḥbūb, from al-ʿAlāʾ ibn Razīn, from Muḥammad ibn Muslim, who said:

I said to Abū Jaʿfar عليه السلام: How is it that ghusl becomes obligatory upon a woman if she sees in sleep that a man has intercourse with her in her private part, while ghusl is not made obligatory upon her if he has intercourse with her short of the private part while awake and she emits fluid? He said: Because she saw in her dream that the man had intercourse with her in her private part, so ghusl became obligatory upon her. But the other only had intercourse with her short of the private part, so ghusl did not become obligatory upon her because he did not insert it. If he had inserted it while awake, ghusl would have become obligatory upon her whether she emitted fluid or did not emit fluid. The basis in this report and what we mentioned in the first report is the same.

key_terms.الْغُسْلُ: ritual bath that becomes obligatory after certain states of janabah
key_terms.الْمَرْأَةِ: the woman who is the subject of the legal ruling
key_terms.دُونَ الْفَرْجِ: short of the private part, indicating non-penetrative intimacy
key_terms.فِي النَّوْمِ: during sleep, referring to what is seen in a dream
key_terms.فِي الْيَقَظَةِ: while awake, referring to an actual waking-state occurrence
key_terms.فِي فَرْجِهَا: in her private part, indicating actual vaginal intercourse
key_terms.لَمْ يُدْخِلْهُ: he did not insert it, meaning penetration did not occur

ai.seo_question: When does ghusl become obligatory for a woman after a sexual dream or physical intimacy?
ai.summary: This hadith explains a legal ruling concerning ghusl for a woman in cases related to sexual experience in sleep and wakefulness. It distinguishes between mere emission and actual penetration, establishing that the obligation of ghusl is tied to the occurrence of intercourse in the private part, whether emission occurs or not.
